concepts.title: Laundromat with wash-and-fold pickup open past 9 pm
concepts.rationale: Laundry is mismatched: none of the 20 laundromats and dry cleaners within 2 km that list hours is open after 9 pm, while the circle has 5 against about 8.2 expected for 38,652 residents. With 80% of households without a vehicle and median household income near $197,069, residents who lack a car and keep late schedules have few options.
concepts.risk: Laundry demand may be served by delivery services and in-building machines, and the 4.2-star average within 2 km sets a high quality bar that a new entrant must match on price and service.

concepts.title: Better-run pharmacy with extended hours and friendly service
concepts.rationale: Pharmacies are poorly served: the 20 rated pharmacies within 2 km average 3.6 stars, and the circle has 17 pharmacies (0.44 per 1,000 residents) against a benchmark of 0.19. Since the demand is already well covered by count, the opening is quality, not volume, and 67% of households rent in a dense population of 38,652.
concepts.risk: With 17 pharmacies already in the circle, including several chain locations, a new pharmacy may struggle to win prescription volume from established chains tied to insurance networks.

concepts.title: Neighborhood convenience store with fresh food and quality service
concepts.rationale: Convenience is poorly served: the 20 rated convenience stores within 2 km average 3.3 stars, yet the circle already has 27 (0.70 per 1,000 residents) against a benchmark of 0.36. Households with no vehicle at 80% and a median age of 36 suggest demand for a higher-quality walkable grocery-convenience hybrid.
concepts.risk: The market already has many convenience stores, so a new one competes on count and may not stand out enough to justify the rent of about $3,501 median.

docs.title: Review of The Dead Rabbit
docs.text: Google review of The Dead Rabbit (5 out of 5, by Peter Shaw, 2 months ago): Great place for food and drinks. The food is excellent. I really liked the Mini spice bag chicken rolls. It a combination of the Irish chicken roll and spice bag in a slider. It’s very good. Lots of Irish signs pics and more.

docs.title: Review of The Dead Rabbit
docs.text:
Google review of The Dead Rabbit (4 out of 5, by Renauld “NauldoNation” Brown, 2 months ago): The Dead Rabbit was a solid stop on our trip, but for us, it didn’t quite live up to all the hype. Don’t get me wrong—it’s a good Irish bar with a great atmosphere, and the Guinness was poured well and went down easy.

One thing I did enjoy was looking over the impressive selection of Irish whiskeys displayed on the top shelves. If you’re a whiskey fan, it’s fun just seeing the variety they have behind the bar.

That said, nothing really stood out as being extraordinary. The drinks were good, the service was good, and the atmosphere was enjoyable, but at the end of the day it felt like a really good Irish pub rather than a must-see destination.

I’d still recommend stopping in if you’re in the area or want to check an iconic New York bar off your list. Just go in with realistic expectations. For us, it was a quality Irish pub with great Guinness and a fantastic whiskey selection—not necessarily a place that completely lived up to the legendary reputation.

docs.title: Review of The Dead Rabbit
docs.text: Google review of The Dead Rabbit (5 out of 5, by Rebecca Gallant, 3 months ago): We visited the upstairs cocktail lounge. Phenomenal cocktails, I tried the Gilded Lady and it did not disappoint! The food was upscale pub food, good flavour. Specifically the side of veggies was a good portion and delicious.

docs.title: Review of The Dead Rabbit
docs.text: Google review of The Dead Rabbit (5 out of 5, by Alex Blake, 3 months ago): The Dead Rabbit Pub NYC is an exceptional spot that captures the authentic charm and atmosphere of a true Irish pub. From the moment you walk in, it feels warm, welcoming, and thoughtfully designed, with a genuine old-world character that makes the experience memorable. The Shepherd’s Pie is a standout dish—comforting, flavorful, and beautifully prepared, with exactly the kind of rich, satisfying quality you hope for in a classic pub meal. Altogether, it delivers a polished and highly enjoyable experience that feels both timeless and distinctively NYC.

docs.title: Review of Joe’s Pizza
docs.text:
Google review of Joe’s Pizza (4 out of 5, by CeeCee’s Little Journey, 3 months ago): Even though I was already full, I couldn’t skip Joe’s Pizza, one of the city’s famous spots. I decided to order just one slice to try. The staff recommended the classic cheese flavor, so I went with that.

The slice was quite nice actually, with thin crust, simple, and satisfying.
It’s the kind of classic pizza that never goes wrong.
On the table, they had cheese, chili flakes, and garlic powder for extra flavor, which making thoughtful for customer to add on based on preference.

The store was crowded, but the turnover was fast, making it a good place for a quick bite.
Overall, a solid experience and I’m giving 4.2/5.

docs.title: Review of Joe’s Pizza
docs.text: Google review of Joe’s Pizza (5 out of 5, by Amy, a month ago): Delicious pizza! If you love NY style thin crust pizza, try Joe’s! The crust is crispy and delicious. We tried a supreme an a caprese. Both were so good! Super crowded, but the line moved quickly.

docs.title: Review of Joe’s Pizza
docs.text: Google review of Joe’s Pizza (5 out of 5, by Suhrob Nuriddinov, 3 months ago): Joe’s Pizza on Fulton Street is exactly what New York pizza should be. Thin, crispy crust, perfectly balanced sauce, and that classic mozzarella stretch that makes every bite satisfying. I stopped in for a quick slice and ended up wishing I had ordered more. The pizza was served fresh, hot, and packed with flavor. The crust had just the right amount of crunch while still being soft and foldable -the true New York way. The ingredients tasted fresh, and you can tell why Joe’s has earned such a strong reputation over the years. The staff was friendly, the service was quick, and the atmosphere had that authentic no-frills NYC pizza vibe that both locals and visitors appreciate. If you’re anywhere near the Financial District and craving real New York pizza, Joe’s Pizza is absolutely worth the stop. One of the best slices in Manhattan, hands down. Highly recommended!

docs.title: Review of Joe’s Pizza
docs.text:
Google review of Joe’s Pizza (4 out of 5, by Harry Zhang, 4 months ago): Very solid pizza. Got the Caprese and Supreme pizza slices, $6.5 a slice, very large.

Thin slice. Very crispy. Fresh ingredients. Solid 8.5/10. Can see why many consider it as the best pizza in New York. I think I’ve had better though. But factoring in the value, it’s very good. It’s very busy but the line moves fast so “one and done justified.”

docs.title: Review of Joe’s Pizza
docs.text:
Google review of Joe’s Pizza (5 out of 5, by Anar Mammadli, 6 months ago): Stopped by Joe’s Pizza for a classic cheese slice and dined in—definitely lived up to the hype. The atmosphere was great, with that iconic, old-school vibe that makes the experience feel authentic.

The pizza itself was exactly what you want from a New York slice: super thin, perfectly crispy crust, and simple but delicious. Every bite was light, crunchy, and full of flavor.

If you’re looking for a true, no-frills pizza spot that delivers on quality, Joe’s is a must-visit. Highly recommend!

docs.title: Review of Fraunces Tavern
docs.text:
Google review of Fraunces Tavern (2 out of 5, by Kenya, 2 months ago): (Long review) I recently visited Fraunces Tavern, and the building itself is absolutely beautiful. It’s full of history and has a fascinating story behind it, which made the experience unique. A big part of my visit was to celebrate my husband’s birthday.

Unfortunately, the food did not meet my expectations, especially considering the prices. The dishes looked delicious when they arrived, but the food was literally as cold as the dining area. The flavor was lacking, and the temperature was a major disappointment. We ordered the mac and cheese, and the cheese wasn’t even melted, it was literally sitting on top of the dish.

The service was okay. Our waitress seemed busy, but the restaurant and museum are located in a very busy area and appear to have a steady flow of customers, so that was understandable.

We did finish our meals and didn’t complain at the time because we didn’t want to make an issue of it. The portions were generous, which was a positive. Overall, I’m glad I got to experience the historic atmosphere and see the restaurant/museum, but I wouldn’t return for the food. It’s definitely worth visiting for the history and the visuals, but my dining experience was disappointing.

docs.title: Review of Fraunces Tavern
docs.text:
Google review of Fraunces Tavern (5 out of 5, by David Green, 2 months ago): If you are looking for an unforgettable night out in New York City that perfectly blends deep American roots with an incredible contemporary vibe, look no further than the historic Fraunces Tavern on a Saturday night.

Stepping into this legendary establishment feels like taking a direct journey back to the late 1700s, but the energy inside is entirely vibrant, welcoming, and alive. We visited this past weekend and wound up celebrating a birthday with a group of three incredible women, and to lean fully into the atmosphere of the venue, they donned colonial-style wigs to look exactly like the founding fathers. It was an absolute hit. Please see pic!

The atmospheric, historic charm of the building paired beautifully with our playful tribute to George Washington’s old stomping grounds.The highlight of the evening was undoubtedly the live music. From 8:00 PM to 11:00 PM, the immensely talented Hannah Ray Teal, in a duo with her talented guitarist Will, took the stage, delivering a captivating performance. Her soulful vocals and fantastic guitar playing filled the room, providing the perfect soundtrack for an exceptional night.

Matching the stellar entertainment was the top-tier hospitality. The staff members were incredibly friendly, fast, and attentive, providing professional service throughout the entire evening. The crowd itself added another wonderful layer to the experience; the tavern attracts a fascinating, diverse mix of international patrons, making for great conversations and a global, upscale energy. Fraunces Tavern delivers on every front—history, exceptional live music, and a crowd that knows how to have a great time. It is the ultimate spot for a legendary NYC night out.

docs.title: Review of Fraunces Tavern
docs.text: Google review of Fraunces Tavern (5 out of 5, by Meagan, 3 months ago): This place was recommended to me by a professor at my university for the museum, but we also knew we had to have dinner at the restaurant for a birthday celebration. It was best atmosphere we could’ve asked for. I’m a huge history buff and really enjoyed learning of this place’s history and its past, even if just through decor or small signs. The food was great— best fish and chips my boyfriend had had, and the lobster and shrimp mac and cheese was delightful. The chocolate peanut butter cake was a great way to end off. We came back to the museum the following day which we also very much enjoyed.

docs.title: Review of Eataly
docs.text: Google review of Eataly (4 out of 5, by Layna Perry, 3 months ago): This is for the Eataly on Liberty. This place is always packed. The food is always good. It’s great for a large group, you don’t feel claustrophobic like some places in Manhattan. We had seven for dinner tonight. I unfortunately did not take photos of the appetizers, or the meal. We did the meatballs, broccolini, calamari; a few glasses of red wine; a salmon, a few steaks, bunch of pastas, and a chicken Milanese. Everyone enjoyed their food. They’re doing something different with the tiramisu since the last time I was there. There are lady fingers in it now, and it’s a bit celebratory how they unwrap it. We also tried the panna cotta, the Amalfi, and limoncello. My only knock was that it might be the dirtiest bathroom I’ve ever used in a restaurant. The bins in each stall were overflowing. I’m going to leave out some details, but it was unpleasant. The labyrinth of the marketplace is such a great vibe. And the location is a huge thumbs up.

docs.title: Review of Eataly

docs.title: Review of McDonald's
docs.text:
Google review of McDonald's (1 out of 5, by RoRo, 6 months ago): I visited this location during my first trip to New York, hoping to use up some loose change and have a simple order. A small tea with hot water and a tea bag. I placed my order at the kiosk, intending to pay in cash, but I wasn’t familiar with how to use the cash machine. So I went to the counter to ask for help and pay directly.
I waited at the front for about 10 minutes, trying not to be a bother, as the cashier seemed busy and not very approachable. When I finally asked for assistance, I was told to go to the machine in the back. I explained that I was having difficulty and just wanted to pay cash for my order (I had the exact amount, $1.62), but instead of helping, she pointed to the work behind her and said she had too much to do.
I completely understand that fast food environments can be busy and demanding. I wasn’t expecting exceptional service, but I was honestly surprised by how dismissive the interaction felt. A little guidance or basic courtesy would have made a big difference.
To be honest, the experience left me feeling so unwelcome that I couldn’t help but think it might have been better to just toss my $1.62 into a fountain and make a wish instead.
As a first-time visitor to New York, this was quite disappointing.

docs.title: Review of O'Hara's
docs.text:
Google review of O'Hara's (5 out of 5, by Jennifer Kopp, a year ago): No better place to go immediately after visiting the WTC area and Museum than O'Hara's! It was a rumor, I believed it, tested it and it was, in fact, true! You feel like you are almost walking into a time capsule the moment you see the door and I won't spoil the surprise by telling you what happens AFTER you open the door.

It is a beautiful spot with so much personality, friendly service and the biggest burger I have ever seen. I couldn't even finish HALF. I think there was an entire pack of pack on it. ;) It was SO good.

Not to mention, really reasonably priced, especially considering it would have fed me three times. I was able to swap out reg fries for sweet potato fries (always a win). The photos of the HAND-WRITTEN menu will tell you everything about the vibe of this unique place..... And the prices are on them. Those portions are HUGE, people! Enjoy!

Will definitely be back!

docs.title: Review of O'Hara's
docs.text: Google review of O'Hara's (5 out of 5, by Nicole Alexandra, 9 months ago): This place has so much personality, it’s a really good option around that area, they have burgers, sandwiches and many other things. docs.title: Review of O'Hara's

docs.title: Review of Manhatta
docs.text:
Google review of Manhatta (5 out of 5, by Cameron, 4 months ago): My husband and I celebrated our first wedding anniversary here at Manhatta. The entire staff was very welcoming and all congratulated us upon arrival. The restaurants is beautiful and situated on the 60th floor. We chose to dine at 7pm so we could see the city before and after sunset.

Our server was extremely knowledgeable of the different wines, I would have thought he was the sommelier. We chose the four course meal paired with wine, and each pairing was excellent. The food was incredible. I would absolutely recommend this restaurant to anyone celebrating a milestone.

docs.title: Review of Manhatta
docs.text: Google review of Manhatta (5 out of 5, by Jas Bonnell, 3 months ago): This has got to be one of the best fine dining, modern restaurants in NYC. I may not be able to say that b/c this was my first time in the city, turning 30 and I read through every review to other places and this was the best. They were #1, WELCOMING! wherever you come from, they make you feel seen, and heard and make you feel like you belong. Like a, “hey , you could be wearing jeans and a T-shirt and we will treat you like a celebrity.” My 30th birthday was all the more special due to this place. I couldn’t have chosen a better place. My husband, my high-school friend and his wife joined me for my special day. I didn’t ask for anything better and the wait staff kept delivering treats and a beautiful little sweet treat with a candle and I felt even more special. Every single dish was a burst of flavor and amazing artistry. You know that saying “so good I could slap my grandma!?” Well, I wanted to line the staff up and give them all high fives and wonderful songs of praises. The views of Manhattan and the other boroughs and the water was an array of magnificence. Reserve your table, make the reservation, eat the food, spend the money, tip the wait staff. 10/10 will recommend to anyone who will listen! Have a beautiful close to your day and thank you for having us!

docs.title: Review of Manhatta
docs.text:
Google review of Manhatta (5 out of 5, by Alaleh - FoodyTO, 4 months ago): We visited Manhatta on a Saturday for my birthday and had a wonderful experience. The restaurant is located on the 60th floor of 28 Liberty Street and offers breathtaking views of Lower Manhattan, the Statue of Liberty, Staten Island, and New York Harbor.

Before our table was ready, we waited in the lounge area and enjoyed the incredible views. A thoughtful touch was the personalized birthday note waiting on our table when we arrived, which made the occasion feel extra special.

The atmosphere was elegant but welcoming, and it was interesting to see that many other guests were also celebrating birthdays and special occasions there.

We came for lunch and ordered the two-course lunch menu. To start, we had the “Beef Tartare” and “Fluke Crudo”, followed by the “Grilled Sea Bass”, “Dry-Aged Burger”, and “Lobster Ravioli” for our mains. For dessert, we enjoyed the “Coconut Mousse” and paired the meal with red wine and the “Land of the Sun” cocktail. The restaurant has an excellent selection of red, white, and sparkling wines.

The service was friendly and attentive without ever making us feel rushed.. We took our time, enjoyed the food, the drinks, and the stunning views, making it a memorable birthday celebration.

docs.title: Review of Manhatta
docs.text:
Google review of Manhatta (5 out of 5, by Linh, 4 months ago): Manhatta has officially become one of my favorite restaurants of all time.

The experience starts with the stunning views from the 60th floor overlooking New York City, but the food and service are what truly make this place special. Every member of the staff was warm, knowledgeable, and attentive without ever being overbearing.

We ordered the four-course menu and every course was outstanding. For the first course, we had the Jonah Crab with asparagus, apple, and sorrel, along with the Bluefin Tuna with jicama, shiso, and white soy vinaigrette. The crab was honestly the best crab dish I’ve ever eaten—sweet, delicate, and perfectly balanced. The tuna was equally impressive, incredibly fresh and beautifully prepared.

For the second course, we chose the Seared Scallop with nduja, watermelon radish, and pea shoots, as well as the Glazed Sweetbreads with morel mushrooms, arugula pesto, and horseradish. Both dishes were expertly executed and packed with flavor.

For our mains, we had the Butter Poached Lobster and the Lamb Loin & Rib. The lobster was excellent, but the real surprise was the Koshihikari rice—it was absolutely amazing and one of the most memorable components of the entire meal. The lamb was perfectly cooked and paired wonderfully with the fava bean pesto, almond, and pecorino.

Dessert was the Pistachio Cake with strawberry and crème fraîche chamomile ice cream, which was a fantastic ending to the meal.

We also enjoyed several mezcal cocktails and wine pairings throughout dinner, all of which complemented the food beautifully.

Between the breathtaking views, exceptional service, creative menu, and unforgettable dishes, Manhatta delivered one of the best dining experiences I’ve had in NYC. Highly recommended, and I can’t wait to come back.

docs.title: Review of Watermark
docs.text:
Google review of Watermark (5 out of 5, by Bella, 6 months ago): Cutest spot ever for a girls’ day out! Pink Pier is exactly what it sounds like. Everything is pink, from the decor to the vibes, and it’s such a fun and photo-worthy destination!

docs.title: Mortimer Building
docs.text:
The Mortimer Building was a 19th-century building located at Wall Street and New Street in the Financial District of Manhattan, New York City. It was built by W.Y. Mortimer beginning
on June 1, 1884, and completed for occupancy in March 1885.  The architect was George B. Post.  It fronted Wall Street for a distance of 57 feet (17 m) and New Street for 65 feet (20 m). Used entirely as an office building, the structure adjoined the New York Stock Exchange Building on the west and south. Tenants included lawyers, brokers, and bankers. The building was used as the general headquarters of the Industrial Workers of the World at its peak between 1912 and 1917.
The New York Stock Exchange acquired the Mortimer Building for $745,000 in December 1918. Reasons for the acquisition included consolidating all the adjuncts of the exchange beneath one roof and the necessity for additional floor space for foreign issues, entertained by the NYSE. The site was valued at $710,000 in February 1920; $745,000 with the building
included. (22 m from the pin.)

docs.title: 14 Wall Street
docs.text:
14 Wall Street, originally the Bankers Trust Company Building, is a skyscraper at the intersection of Wall Street and Nassau Street in the Financial District of Manhattan in New York City. The building is 540 feet (160 m) tall, with 32 usable floors. The original 540-foot tower is at the southeastern corner of the site, and a shorter annex wraps around the original tower.
The original tower was erected on the site of the Stevens Building at 12–14 Wall Street and the Gillender Building at 16 Wall Street. It was built in 1910–1912 and was designed by Trowbridge & Livingston in the neoclassical style as the headquarters for Bankers Trust. A 25-story addition with Art Deco detailing, designed by Shreve, Lamb & Harmon, was constructed in 1931–1933 to replace three other structures. After new buildings for Bankers Trust were erected in 1962 and 1974, the company moved employees away from 14 Wall Street, and eventually sold the building in 1987.
14 Wall Street's tower incorporates a seven-story pyramidal roof inspired by the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus. The interior of the building contained numerous amenities that were considered state-of-the-art at the time of its construction; the first three floors were used as Bankers Trust's headquarters, while the rest were rented to tenants. A notable building in Manhattan's skyline in the early 20th century, the building was featured prominently in Bankers Trust's early imagery. The building was designated a New York City landmark in 1997.… (39 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Wall Street station (IRT Lexington Avenue Line)
docs.text:
The Wall Street station (referred to on some strip maps as Wall Street–Broadway) is a station on the IRT Lexington Avenue Line of the New York City Subway. The station is located at the intersection of Broadway and Wall Street in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan. It is served by the 4 train at all times and the 5 train at all times except late nights.
The Wall Street station was constructed for the Interborough Rapid Transit Company (IRT) as part of the city's first subway line, which was approved in 1900. Construction of the tunnel around the Wall Street station was complicated by the shallow foundations of the nearby Trinity Church, as well as the need to avoid disrupting the street surface of Broadway. The station opened on June 12, 1905, as an extension of the original line. The station's platforms were lengthened in the late 1950s, and it was renovated in the 1970s and 2000s.
The Wall Street station contains two side platforms and two tracks, and it was built with tile and mosaic decorations. The platforms contain exits to Broadway's intersections with Wall and Rector Streets, outside Trinity Church, and into the basements of several buildings. An additional passageway extends east to an out-of-system connection with the Broad Street station and the basement of 28 Liberty Street. The original station interior is a New York City designated landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places. (42 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Manhattan Life Insurance Building
docs.text: The Manhattan Life Insurance Building was an early skyscraper on Broadway in the Financial District of Manhattan, New York City, United States. At 348 ft (106 m) tall, it was the first skyscraper to pass 330 ft (100 m) in Manhattan. (44 m from the pin.)

docs.title: 1 Wall Street
docs.text:
1 Wall Street (also known as the Irving Trust Company Building, the Bank of New York Building, and the BNY Mellon Building) is a 654-foot-tall (199 m) Art Deco skyscraper in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan, New York City, United States. The building, which occupies a full city block, consists of two sections. The original 50-story building was designed by Ralph Thomas Walker of the firm Voorhees, Gmelin and Walker and constructed between 1929 and 1931 for Irving Trust, an early-20th-century American bank. A 28-story annex to the south (later expanded to 36 stories) was designed by the successor firm Voorhees, Walker, Smith, Smith & Haines and built between 1963 and 1965.
The limestone facade consists of slight inwardly-curved bays with fluting to resemble curtains. On the lower stories are narrow windows and elaborate entrances. The massing of 1 Wall Street incorporates numerous small setbacks, and there are chamfers at the corners of the original building. The top of the original building consists of a freestanding tower with fluted windowless bays. The facade of the annex is crafted in a style reminiscent of the original structure. The original building has an ornate lobby, known as the Red Room, with colored mosaics. The 10th through 45th floors were originally rented to tenants, while the other floors contained offices, lounges, and other spaces for Irving Trust.
At the time of its construction, 1 Wall Street occupied what was one of the most valuable plots in… (44 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Lower Manhattan
docs.text:
Lower Manhattan, also known as Downtown Manhattan, is the southernmost part of the New York City borough of Manhattan. The area is the historical birthplace of New York City and in the 17th and 18th centuries composed the entirety of the city. Lower Manhattan serves as the seat of government of both Manhattan and the entire City of New York. Because there are no municipally defined boundaries for the area, a precise population cannot be quoted, but several sources have suggested that it was one of the fastest-growing locations in New York City between 2010 and 2020, related to the influx of young adults and significant development of new housing units.
Despite various definitions of Lower Manhattan, they generally include all of Manhattan Island south of 14th Street, with the 
Bowling Green and the Battery near the southern end. Anchored by Wall Street and the Financial District in Lower Manhattan, New York City is the leading global center  for finance and fintech. The Financial District houses the New York Stock Exchange, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and other major financial institutions. A center of culture and tourism, Lower Manhattan is home to many of New York City's most iconic structures, including New York City Hall, the Woolworth Building, the Stonewall Inn, the Charging Bull of Wall Street, and One World Trade Center, the tallest skyscraper in the Western Hemisphere. (51 m from the pin.)

docs.title: New York Stock Exchange Building
docs.text:
The New York Stock Exchange Building (also NYSE Building) is the headquarters of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), located in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan in New York City. It is composed of two connected structures occupying much of the city block bounded by Wall Street, Broad Street, New Street, and Exchange Place. The central section of the block contains the original structure at 18 Broad Street, designed in the Classical Revival style by George B. Post. The northern section contains a 23-story office annex at 11 Wall Street, designed by Trowbridge & Livingston in a similar style.
The marble facade of 18 Broad Street contains colonnades facing east toward Broad Street and west toward New Street, both atop two-story podiums. The Broad Street colonnade, an icon of the NYSE, contains a pediment designed by John Quincy Adams Ward and Paul Wayland Bartlett, depicting commerce and industry. The facade of 11 Wall Street is simpler in design but contains architectural details similar to those at 18 Broad Street. Behind the colonnades at 18 Broad Street is the main trading floor, a 72-foot-tall (22 m) rectangular space. An additional trading floor, nicknamed the Garage, is at 11 Wall Street. There are offices and meeting rooms in the upper stories of 18 Broad Street and 11 Wall Street.
The NYSE had occupied the site on Broad Street since 1865 but had to expand its previous building several times. The structure at 18 Broad Street was erected between 1901 and 1903.… (64 m from the pin.)

docs.title: New York Armory Raid
docs.text: New York Armory Raid was an action by Sons of Liberty on April 23, 1775, in the early days of the American Revolutionary War. The raid was on the British soldiers' munitions, military supplies and stores held in New York City. The armory became a target for American patriots shortly after the outbreak of the Revolutionary War on April 19, 1775. (66 m from the pin.)

docs.title: American Surety Building
docs.text:
The American Surety Building (also known as the Bank of Tokyo Building or 100 Broadway) is an office building and early skyscraper at Pine Street and Broadway in the Financial District of Manhattan in New York City, across from Trinity Church. The building was designed in a Neo-Renaissance style by Bruce Price with a later expansion by Herman Lee Meader. It is 388 feet (118 m) tall, with either 23 or 26 stories. It was one of Manhattan's first buildings with steel framing and curtain wall construction.
The American Surety Building contains a facade of Maine granite. Its articulation consists of three horizontal sections similar to the components of a column, namely a base, shaft, and capital, making the American Surety Building one of the earliest New York City skyscrapers to feature such a layout. The facade contains several ornamental features, including sculptural elements designed by J. Massey Rhind. In addition, the American Surety Building uses an interior skeleton of structural steel, as well as a cantilevered steel structure for its foundations.
The building was erected between 1894 and 1896 as a 21-story structure, which was the second tallest building in New York City when completed. Between 1920 and 1922, an annex was built to designs by Meader, increasing the floor area and adding two stories to the building. A later tenant, the Bank of Tokyo, hired Kajima International to restore the lower 13 stories between 1973 and 1975. The American Surety Building was made a… (67 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Gillender Building
docs.text:
The Gillender Building was an early skyscraper in the Financial District of Manhattan in New York City. It stood on the northwest corner of Wall Street and Nassau Street, on a narrow strip of land measuring 26 by 73 feet (7.9 m × 22.3 m). At the time of its completion in 1897, the Gillender Building was, depending on ranking methods, the fourth- or eighth-tallest structure in New York City.
The Gillender Building was designed by Charles I. Berg and Edward H. Clark, and rose 273 feet (83 m) with 20 stories, comprising 17 floors in the main body and three floors in a cupola. The building contained a fully wind-braced steel frame with masonry infill, and included twelve columns atop three caisson foundations. On its completion, it was praised as an engineering novelty. It attracted attention for its disproportionate height and its low total rentable area of only about 30,000 square feet (2,800 m2).
The Gillender Building was occupied by financial firms through its uneventful 13-year existence and was perceived as economically obsolete from the start. In 1909, financial institutions began rapidly expanding their properties within the Financial District, and that December, the building was sold to Bankers Trust for a then-record price of $822 per square foot ($8,850/m2). The Gillender Building was demolished between April and June 1910 to make way for Bankers Trust's 39-story tower at 14 Wall Street, and much of the material from the building was saved. At the time, the Gillender… (68 m from the pin.)

docs.title: New York Stock Exchange
docs.text: The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE, nicknamed "the Big Board") is an American stock exchange headquartered at the New York Stock Exchange Building in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan in New York City. It is the largest stock exchange in the world by market capitalization, exceeding in January 2026. The NYSE is owned by Intercontinental Exchange, an American holding company that it also lists (ticker symbol ICE). Previously, it was part of NYSE Euronext (NYX), which was formed by the NYSE's 2007 merger with Euronext. (69 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Money to Burn (performance art)
docs.text:
Money to Burn was a work of performance art executed on June 22, 2010, in which Dread Scott burned $171 in US dollar bills in front of the New York Stock Exchange.
Scott filmed himself repeatedly singing "money to bur-rn, money to burn" while burning one bill at a time with a Zippo lighter, both from the $250 in small bills attached to his clothes, and from bills solicited from passers-by.
Describing the performance, Scott said "I did the one thing you shouldn't do with money: burn it. Burning it is the one thing that everyone thinks is just crazy. But I was doing in extremely small form what happens on the stock exchange daily on a much grander scale."
After 25 minutes, the New York Police Department intervened and issued Scott a summons for disorderly conduct, which he fought in court. (69 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Broad Street station (BMT Nassau Street Line)
docs.text:
The Broad Street station is a station on the BMT Nassau Street Line of the New York City Subway at the intersection of Broad and Wall Streets in the Financial District of Manhattan. It serves as the southern terminal for J trains at all times and for Z trains during rush hours in the peak direction.
The station was built as part of the Dual Contracts, signed between the Brooklyn Rapid Transit Company (later reorganized as the Brooklyn–Manhattan Transit Corporation, or BMT) and the city in 1913. The Nassau Street Line was one of the last lines to be completed under the Dual Contracts, and construction did not proceed until James Walker was elected as mayor of New York City in 1926. This station opened on May 29, 1931, as part of the final portion of the Nassau Street Line. Despite being under Broad and Nassau Streets, with Wall Street as the cross-street, this station was named after Broad Street to prevent confusion with other stations. Between 1990 and 2015, Broad Street was only open on weekdays and weekday nights. (73 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Statue of John Watts
docs.text: An outdoor bronze sculpture depicting U.S. Congressman John Watts by George Edwin Bissell is installed in the Trinity Church Cemetery outside Manhattan's Trinity Church, in the U.S. state of New York. It was erected by Watt's grandson, John Watts de Peyster, in 1893. (74 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Hanover Bank Building
docs.text: The Hanover Bank Building or Hanover National Bank Building was an early skyscraper at the southwest corner of Pine Street and Nassau Street in Lower Manhattan, New York City. It was built in 1901-1903 and demolished in 1931. (75 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Statue of George Washington (Wall Street)
docs.text: George Washington is a large bronze sculpture of George Washington by John Quincy Adams Ward, installed on the front steps of Federal Hall National Memorial on Wall Street in New York City. (77 m from the pin.)

docs.title: 23 Wall Street
docs.text:
23 Wall Street (also known as the J.P. Morgan Building) is a four-story office building in the Financial District of Manhattan in New York City, United States. Located at the southeast corner of Wall Street and Broad Street, it was designed by Trowbridge & Livingston in the neoclassical style and constructed from 1913 to 1914. It was originally the headquarters of J.P. Morgan & Co. Since the late 2000s, the building has remained unoccupied for long periods, although it has occasionally been used for events.
The building has a facade of ashlar masonry and pink Tennessee marble. The first floor consists of a piano nobile over a low basement; above are the second story, the main cornice, and two more stories. After its completion, the building became known as the headquarters of J.P. Morgan & Co.—the "House of Morgan"—although its exterior was never signed with the Morgan name. The banking room, which took up nearly the entire ground floor, included offices and was used for banking transactions. This space was designed with a domed, coffered ceiling and, later, a large crystal chandelier. Mechanical systems and vaults were in the basement, and executive offices were placed on the upper floors.
23 Wall Street replaced the Drexel Building, which was the banking headquarters for J.P. Morgan & Co.'s predecessor Drexel, Morgan & Co. When the building was damaged during the Wall Street bombing in 1920, J.P. Morgan & Co. refused to make repairs, in defiance of the bombing's… (88 m from the pin.)

docs.title: United States Custom House (New York City)
docs.text: The United States Custom House, sometimes referred to as the New York Custom House, was the place where the United States Customs Service collected federal customs duties on imported goods within New York City. (92 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Federal Hall
docs.text:
Federal Hall was the first capitol building of the United States established under the Constitution. Serving as the meeting place of the First United States Congress and the site of George Washington's first presidential inauguration, the building was located on Wall Street facing the northern end of Broad Street in Lower Manhattan, New York City, from 1703 to 1812. The site is occupied by the Federal Hall National Memorial, a Greek Revival–style building completed in 1842 as the New York Custom House. The National Park Service now operates the building as a national memorial commemorating the historic events that occurred at Federal Hall.
The original structure on the site was built from 1699 to 1703 as New York's second city hall. The building hosted the 1765 Stamp Act Congress, before the American Revolution. After the United States became an independent nation, it served as the meeting place for the Congress of the Confederation, the nation's first central government under the Articles of Confederation, from 1785 to 1789, and the building was expanded and updated. With the establishment of the United States federal government in 1789, it hosted the 1st Congress and the inauguration of George Washington as the nation's first president. In addition to other seminal legislation, the 1st Congress adopted the plan to create Washington, D.C. as the national capital, and to move to Philadelphia in the meantime.  After congress left in 1790, the old hall was demolished in… (92 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Stock Exchange Luncheon Club
docs.text:
The Stock Exchange Luncheon Club was a members-only dining club, on the seventh floor of the New York Stock Exchange Building at 11 Wall Street in Manhattan. The club was founded on August 3, 1898,  and moved from 70 Broadway to 11 Wall Street when the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) opened its new building in 1903.  It closed on April 28, 2006, after more than a century of service.
The club had an inaugural membership of 200, with a "long waiting list", when it first opened as the Luncheon Club at 70 Broadway and 15 New Street, Manhattan.
Joseph L. Searles III, who became the first African American member of the NYSE when he joined in 1970, said that his "biggest fear...was where would I sit in the luncheon club?". The situation was resolved when Searles was given his own table by the club, and he dined alone for a while.
A ladies' restroom was installed in the club as late as 1987, some twenty years after women were first admitted to the NYSE.
In 1999, the club had more than 1,400 members, and was lavishly decorated with various animal heads, most shot by members on safari.
In August 2001, the Stock Exchange Luncheon Club served as the venue for the presentation of custom-made motorized wheelchairs to 17 quadraplegic in-patients of a local hospital for paralyzed people.  A fund-raising event was held by the New York City Police Foundation at the club in November 2003. Following security measures put in place at the NYSE, after the September 11 attacks, the club became less… (93 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Commercial Cable Company Building
docs.text:
The Commercial Cable Company Building was an early skyscraper at 20–24 Broad Street Extension in Manhattan, New York City. Built for the Commercial Cable Company, it started construction in 1896 and was completed in 1897. It was designed by Harding & Gooch. Its height was 92.7 m (304 ft) and it was 22 stories tall. The building, like many of its contemporaries, was built in a historicist style, richly decorated. Two domes were designed on top.
The building adjoined the New York Stock Exchange. The Exchange leased the western portions of the first three floors in 1926, which were remodeled to include an trading floor.
It stood for half a century and was demolished in 1954. A 27-story modern office building was built in its place. (93 m from the pin.)

docs.title: New York Law Institute
docs.text: The New York Law Institute is the oldest circulating law library in New York City and is open to Institute members and to scholars of history and the law. (94 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Fearless Girl
docs.text:
Fearless Girl is a bronze sculpture by Kristen Visbal of a 4-foot-high (1.2 m) girl standing in a self-confident pose. It is located in New York City on Broad Street across from the New York Stock Exchange Building in the Financial District of Manhattan.
Fearless Girl was commissioned by State Street Investment Management, formerly State Street Global Advisors (SSGA), a large asset management company, to promote gender diversity initiatives and an index fund focused on gender-diverse companies with a relatively high percentage of women in senior leadership. As of 2025, State Street quietly backed away from its commitment to diversity, and the statue's future remains uncertain.
The statue was first installed at the northern tip of Bowling Green on Broadway, facing the sculpture Charging Bull on March 7, 2017, in anticipation of International Women's Day on the following day. Following complaints from Charging Bull sculptor Arturo Di Modica, Fearless Girl was removed in November 2018 and relocated to its Broad Street location the following month. A plaque with footprints was placed on the original site of Fearless Girl. (95 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Trinity Church Cemetery
docs.text:
The parish of Trinity Church has three separate burial grounds associated with it in the New York City borough of Manhattan. The first, Trinity Churchyard, is located in Lower Manhattan at 74 Trinity Place, near Wall Street and Broadway. Alexander Hamilton and his wife Elizabeth Schuyler Hamilton, Albert Gallatin, and Robert Fulton are buried in the downtown Trinity Churchyard.
The second Trinity parish burial ground is the St. Paul's Chapel Churchyard, which is also located in Lower Manhattan, six blocks (roughly 440 yards (400 m)) north of Trinity Church. It was established in 1766. Both of these churchyards are closed to new burials.
Trinity's third place of burial, Trinity Church Cemetery and Mausoleum, located in Hamilton Heights in Upper Manhattan, is one of the few active burial sites in Manhattan. Trinity Church Cemetery and Mausoleum is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is the burial place of notable people including John James Audubon, John Jacob Astor IV, Mayor Edward I. Koch, Governor John Adams Dix, Ralph Ellison, and Eliza Jumel. In 1823, all burials south of Canal Street became forbidden by New York City due to city crowding, yellow fever, and other public health fears.
After considering locations in the Bronx and portions of the then-new Green-Wood Cemetery, in 1842 Trinity Parish purchased the plot of land now bordered by 153rd Street, 155th Street, Amsterdam Avenue, and Riverside Drive to establish the Trinity Church Cemetery and… (98 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Trinity Church (Manhattan)
docs.text:
Trinity Church is a historic parish in the Episcopal Diocese of New York. The church is located at 89 Broadway opposite Wall Street, in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan in New York City. Known for its centuries of history, prominent location, distinguished architecture and bountiful endowment, Trinity's congregation is said to be "high church", its activities based on the traditions of the Episcopal Church and the worldwide Anglican Communion in missionary outreach, and fellowship. In addition to its main church, Trinity parish maintains two chapels: St. Paul's Chapel, also in Lower Manhattan, and the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion on Governors Island. The Church of the Intercession, the Trinity Chapel Complex and many other of Manhattan's Episcopal congregations were once part of Trinity parish. Columbia University was founded on the church's grounds as King's College in 1754.
The building Trinity Church has occupied since 1846, designed by Richard Upjohn in the Gothic Revival style, is the third church constructed for the parish. Trinity's first church building was a single-story rectangular structure with tall steeple facing the Hudson River, which was constructed in 1698 and destroyed in the Great New York City Fire of 1776. After using St. Paul's Chapel, the parish's second building was built on Broadway at Wall Street and was consecrated in 1790. The third church was erected on the second building's site from 1839 to 1846 and was the tallest building in… (99 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Wall Street bombing
docs.text:
The Wall Street bombing was an act of terrorism on Wall Street at 12:01 pm on Thursday, September 16, 1920. The blast killed 30 people immediately, and another eight later died of wounds that they sustained in the blast. There were 143 seriously injured, and the total number of injured was in the hundreds.
The bombing was never solved, although investigators and historians believe it was carried out by Galleanists, a group responsible for a series of bombings the previous year. (101 m from the pin.)

docs.title: 65 Broadway
docs.text:
65 Broadway, formerly the American Express Building, is a building on Broadway between Morris and Rector Streets in the Financial District of Manhattan in New York City. The 21-story concrete and steel-frame structure, an office building, was designed by J. Lawrence Aspinwall of the firm Renwick, Aspinwall & Tucker in the Neoclassical style. 65 Broadway extends westward through an entire block, to Trinity Place. Its most prominent feature is its H-shaped building plan, with light courts located between its wings.
The financial services company American Express had been located at the site of 65 Broadway since 1874, and purchased the lot in 1903. The current building was constructed in 1916–1917. It was the headquarters of American Express until 1974, and also contained the offices of other firms. After American Express moved out, 65 Broadway was occupied by American Bureau of Shipping and then by Standard & Poor's; as of 2019, Chetrit Group owns the building. The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the building as an official New York City landmark in 1995. It is also a contributing property to the Wall Street Historic District, a National Register of Historic Places district created in 2007. (106 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Equitable Life Building (Manhattan)
docs.text:
The Equitable Life Assurance Building, also known as the Equitable Life Building, was the headquarters of the Equitable Life Assurance Society of the United States, at 120 Broadway in Manhattan, New York. Arthur Gilman and Edward H. Kendall designed the building, with George B. Post as a consulting engineer. The Equitable Life Building was made of brick, granite, and iron, and was originally built with seven above-ground stories and two basement levels, with a height of at least 130 feet (40 m). An expansion in 1885 brought the total height to 155 feet (47 m) and nine stories.
Construction began in 1868 and was completed in 1870 under the leadership of Equitable's president Henry Baldwin Hyde. It was the world's first office building to feature passenger elevators and consequently became successful attracting tenants. The Equitable Life Building was expanded numerous times; after the construction of annexes during the late 1880s, the building occupied its entire block, bounded by Broadway and Cedar, Pine and Nassau streets. Although it was advertised as fireproof, the Equitable Life Building was destroyed in a 1912 fire that killed six people. The 40-story Equitable Building was completed on the site in 1915. (112 m from the pin.)

docs.title: 15 Broad Street

15 Broad Street (formerly known as the Equitable Trust Building) is a residential condominium and former office building in the Financial District of Manhattan, New York City, on the eastern side of Broad Street between Wall Street and Exchange Place. It has entrances at 51 Exchange Place and 35 Wall Street.
It was completed in 1928 and ranked among the 20 largest office buildings in the world in 1931. (112 m from the pin.)

docs.text:
Google review of Alba Dry Cleaners & Tailoring (5 out of 5, by Vivian Ly, 5 months ago): I would actually give them a 8/5 if I could! They got a tragic pizza grease stain out of a Blueberry trench for a reasonable price.

I was carrying a pizza box home far away from my coat and at one point, I looked down and all of the grease from a closed box had poured all over my trench coat. I called seven different dry cleaners. Most were unhelpful, and threw out insane prices the moment they heard Burburry. I had a shop quote me $245 as a starting point, and tell me that there were no guarantees.

I walked into Alba, and the staff just said they would handle it and if they couldn’t get it out, I didn’t need to pay. They didn’t try to alarm me, or make things seem worse than they were like every other place. They kept it really simple, and asked if I was willing to give them a chance. I’m deeply appreciative of how quickly they got it out, how easy they made the process, and that they even delivered the coat back to my apartment for $45. I couldn’t recommend this place over and over again and will definitely be coming back.

He's been on a boat for several weeks and needed to do his laundry/have clean uniforms, but his time in port was limited and on a holiday weekend. We are so thankful for the great service and care that was given!

docs.text:
Google review of G & G Cleaners (1 out of 5, by N K, a year ago): I can’t believe this place is even in business. They destroy every single clothing item that passes through their doors. Ask for dry cleaning? They’ll shrink your clothes into doll sizes. Drop off whites? You’ll pick them up with mysterious yellow stains that weren’t there before. They don’t deodorize, they don’t clean properly, and they certainly don’t take responsibility.

This isn’t a “cleaners,” it’s a clothing graveyard. Their idea of “professional service” is treating your wardrobe like a science experiment gone wrong. I’ve seen better results tossing my clothes into a puddle on Houston Street.

The customer service is just as bad—condescending, dismissive, and unapologetic. They’ll smile while handing back a ruined item as if it’s normal. The only thing consistent about this place is the disappointment.

If you value your clothing (or basic human respect), avoid G&G Cleaners like the plague. Honestly, someone should shut this place down before they ruin anyone else’s wardrobe.

docs.title: Review of G & G Cleaners
docs.text:
Google review of G & G Cleaners (1 out of 5, by Blue Gaming, 2 years ago): If I could give zero stars, I would. My experience with G and G Cleaners was nothing short of a scammy disaster from start to finish. I brought in a simple skirt for a basic hem, expecting professional service and reasonable pricing. What I got was an absolute rip-off and a masterclass in bait-and-switch tactics.

First, they quoted me a modest price for the work, which seemed fair at $40. But when I came to pick up the skirt, the price had *magically* doubled! The excuse? Some nonsense about “additional adjustments” that were never discussed or authorized. I challenged the inflated price, but they stood their ground, refusing to release the skirt until I paid up. They know exactly what they’re doing—hold your items hostage and extort as much money as they can.

But it gets worse. When I finally got the skirt back (after begrudgingly paying the absurd fee), I discovered the quality of work was atrocious. Crooked stitches, uneven hemline—honestly, I’ve seen better craftsmanship from a first-day sewing student. It’s clear they couldn’t care less about delivering quality, just cashing in.

To top it all off, the owner’s attitude was condescending and downright rude. He dismissed my concerns and acted as if I should be grateful he even deigned to work on my skirt. Save yourself the trouble (and a lot of money) and steer clear of this place. They’re not tailors—they’re con artists in disguise.

This was all done with a super quick turnaround so I already have my dress back. Thanks to the team at Bridgestone for addressing all my concerns and providing me with excellent service the second time around, I'm glad I gave them the chance to remedy the situation - they went above and beyond.

I came here to get my wedding dress cleaned because my bridal boutique recommended them. They were originally very responsive when I sent in an inquiry but the service dropped off throughout the process and when I made an appointment with Nina, the wedding gown specialist, to get my dress assessed in person and a more accurate quote she did not show (I don't live that close to this location). I eventually did get an estimate over text and went ahead with the cleaning because they were the most affordable option. I got my dress back in a relatively timely manner but there was a small tear on the hem, a random red stain on the inside, and the bag my wedding dress was returned in had some sort of black oil on the outside that stained my garment bag I transported everything in. It was lucky that I noticed it so I was super careful removing my dress from the bag but imagine if it had gotten on my dress!

The overall cleaning job was fine and all the staff at the location were super friendly and kind but for $500+ cleaning service I would expect a little more care. Not to mention when I reached out noting these things, I was essentially ghosted. It's just unfortunate because there aren't really good alternative options for wedding dress cleaning that don't cost a fortune in the city so... just be extra careful when you get your items back and make sure to check the outside of the garment back you get back!

docs.text:
Google review of Daily Bubble Laundromat Inc. (1 out of 5, by Jennifer Bath, 4 months ago): I was surprised by the positive reviews for this place, because our experience was deeply concerning. We suspected our clothes were not actually being washed - items came back smelling like fabric softener but not clean, and clothes with stain remover on them still had the stain remover residue, which came right off when we washed them ourselves.

So we tested it. On a second visit, we deliberately added stain remover to three items in a large load before drop-off. None of the stain remover had been washed off when we got the clothes back - stain remover dissolves immediately on contact with water, so if these items had been through a wash cycle, it would have come off. It did not. The clothes just smelled like fabric softener, masking the fact they had not been cleaned at all.

To make matters worse, we had left quarters at the bottom of our bag from a previous trip - they were gone when we got our clothes back.

To their credit, they did wash our undergarments properly. But we cannot recommend this laundromat for a full-service wash. If you need clean clothes, find a self-service laundromat - we found a great one in Chinatown.

Google review of 7-Eleven (1 out of 5, by Rishita Mehta, a year ago): Absolutely unacceptable customer service. I visited this 7-Eleven and purchased a pack of AA batteries, only to realize minutes later that I actually needed AAA. I returned within five minutes, with the receipt in hand and the product completely unopened.

Despite this, the staff refused to exchange the batteries, claiming that “no exchange on electronic cigarettes” also applied to batteries — which is nowhere stated or implied. That’s not only misleading, it’s borderline gaslighting.

Trying to pass off “electronics” as part of a “no exchange on electronic cigarettes” policy is absurd. If you’re going to deny returns, have the decency to post it clearly and be honest with customers instead of making up rules on the spot.

I won’t be returning to this location, and I’d strongly advise others to check everything carefully — and not expect fairness or accountability if you need help.

Google review of Duane Reade (5 out of 5, by F F, 5 months ago): I have been to many Duane Reades/Walgreens locations across this great nation. This one’s satisfactorily stocked and does a fine job with my prescriptions. But more importantly:

I have seen tired cashiers, indifferent cashiers, cashiers who looked right through me, throughout my life. And then I met Nigel.

Nigel doesn't just work at this Walgreens . He *is* this Walgreens. The man is one of the most amicable people I have ever encountered behind a retail counter. One time when I really needed headphones, he actually hunted them down digging through everything back behind the counter until he found exactly what I needed. That kind of effort is rare. That kind of effort is Nigel.

But here's the kicker. In 23 years of checking out at retailers, I have never signed up for a loyalty card when prompted at the register. It always felt like a trap. A hustle. Which is why I’d always say no.

Nigel asked me once. With a smile. And then proceeded to make the single most compelling case for a loyalty card I have ever heard in my life. I don’t even fully remember what he said. I just know that by the end of it I was nodding, gave him my phone number, my zip code, and frankly would have handed him the keys to my apartment if he'd asked.

Walgreens corporate, if you are reading this: promote this man. Make him regional manager. Make him VP of Customer Experience. Make him CEO. Make him whatever you need to make him because whatever Nigel is doing, it is the entire point of retail. He is the reason the loyalty program exists. He is the reason this location gets five stars.

docs.text: Google review of CVS (1 out of 5, by Annie Wu, 6 months ago): Be aware! This is the worst pharmacy and stay away! Our patient went yesterday to get her prescription but was told no medication for her and she needed to call the doctor for new prescription.  However, her prescription was just sent on 3/11/26, and it doesn’t make sense, so we called this CVS.  We were told the medication was cancelled by a pharmacist on 3/11 due to confusion but never confirmed with our office.  I, as a prescriber, wanted to find out what happened. After waiting on the phone for 15 minutes, came the manager who’s very arrogant claimed the medication was cancelled due to “another medication also prescribed on the same day, they were considered as the same medications”.  Obviously she’s not a medical professional and I tried to correct what she said was not true. Then she said “you don’t listen to me then we won’t fill the medication for the patient.” And I heard someone next to her laughed out very loud as if they nailed the situation.  How low was that! Use a patient’s wellbeing to threaten! How could a person like this works as a manger at CVS pharmacy!  No sense of caring, compassion or sympathy at all!  Fortunately there are many other pharmacies that doctors and patients can choose, we definitely won’t send our patients to pharmacy like this anymore!

Google review of CVS (1 out of 5, by SRG, 4 months ago): The African American lady working the photo service counter on 5/27/2026 has a horrible attitude.

I came to print an existing photo and her back was turned to me for at least 5 minutes although she heard me making enquiries about where to go. When she finally acknowledged my existence, she sent me to the kiosks. The kiosks had no Bluetooth option and the USB connection also did not work. One of her colleagues tried to assist me by directing me to the CVS website to place an order as an alternative. Google review of CVS Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Rick Yalie, 4 months ago): As always my Rx were filled and ready at the designated time. In addition, the self scanning monitors are more efficient and easier to use than when they first introduced.

However one major issue has been overlooked, and rather unexpected from a pharmacy by the use of the self help.

Health experts estimate that approximately 80% of common infectious diseases are spread through direct or indirect hand contact. Touching contaminated surfaces and then touching your eyes, nose, or mouth is the primary way these germs enter your body.

Given that everyone is directed to the self help scanner for check in, and the likelihood that the majority of Rx for pickup are from clients that maybe carriers of contagious illnesses, their should be alcohol pads available for quick cleaning, especially for seniors who are more vulnerable.

I was surprised that almost every time at check in,  I have seen the finger prints from prior users. While my experiences at CVS are always a 10+, I thought highlighting this issue merited sharing.

She wears a sour expression all day long, looking as if someone owes her millions. Customers are put in a bad mood the moment they walk through the door first thing in the morning.

docs.title: Review of Downtown Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Downtown Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Colin Milne, 3 months ago): Staff were helpful. I found the pharmacy was more of a corner shop but this was the add on to the pharmacy.

docs.title: Review of Downtown Pharmacy
docs.text:
Google review of Downtown Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Christopher, 11 months ago): By far one of the best old school pharmacies in Manhattan insofar as treatment of their patients like family with new school like technology, they make everything from insurance to delivery to your home seamless.
There have been times where they have delivered to my home. Multiple times a day, not only my pharmaceuticals but also medical supplies. They have a wonderful selection. And they can get anything in within 24 hours. Do yourself a favor. Ever skip the line at those big impersonal, national pharmacies and do your business with downtown. You won't be sorry. We've used them for the past three years.And We are going to be customers for life.

docs.title: Review of Downtown Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Downtown Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Julian, 9 months ago): Really great pharmacy as they have 50¢ chip bags and etc. however, many of the drinks and big chip bags are overpriced as I recall a bottle of Gatorade being $2.75 when I could get it from the Indian cart for $1

Appreciate your attention and kindness.

docs.title: Review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy (2 out of 5, by Yasmeen Omer, 9 months ago): This pharmacy has been great for my dad. But I can’t say I’ve ever had a good or easy experience with them. The wait is regularly around 30min in a very cramped, messy space full of old products covered in dust and sticky residue. I wasn’t going to write a review, but since October they have not refilled a prescription for me. I have gone in at least 10 times since then to see what is going on and get a run around. I never get the same answer. And it’s always “not their fault.” But it is their fault that they don’t communicate properly with their customers about their prescriptions. I will be looking for a more professional pharmacy or prescription service for myself. I no longer trust them to take care of my prescription needs.

docs.title: Review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Daniel Wray, 8 months ago): I don't live close anymore, but this is the best pharmacy in soho due to the staffs empathy and kindness. Not just with me, with everyone who I've seen come in. They will specially order supplements for you, and even call you when it comes in. The pharmacist gave me the stores number (that specifically would be the number to come up, to differentiate from spam), as well as taking my number down, not just on a computer, they have a pen and paper list/system specifically for these type of calls. They by far have the most diverse array of medical otc devices and supplements. 10/5

docs.title: Review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by thalia kelly, 4 months ago): This is by far the best pharmacy I’ve ever dealt with. The staff is kind and empathetic & when you call you get through to them immediately (zero automation). The owner was the first person to wish me a happy birthday this year 🥹

docs.title: Review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Darius Opada, 7 months ago): So happy I found this pharmacy. My medication is something difficult to find across NYC but through them I was able to find them. Yes, they might not be as big as other pharmacies but they do their best and give the best that they have.

docs.title: Review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy
docs.text:
Google review of Xpress Lane Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by JC, 10 months ago): People usually only write reviews when service is terrible or exceptional — and this pharmacy is truly exceptional. This is hands-down the best pharmacy I’ve ever dealt with, whether commercial or private. The owner (who is genuinely funny and welcoming) and the entire staff are consistently professional, kind, and incredibly helpful. They always go out of their way to assist.
Outstanding service, every single time. Thank you Xpress Lane.

docs.text: Google review of CVS Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Ronald Madson, a year ago): I had a problem with refilling a prescription.   The pharmacist proposed a workable solution.  The CVS pharmacy in Brooklyn Heights has a history of pleasant, intelligent staffing.

docs.title: Review of CVS Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of CVS Pharmacy (1 out of 5, by Brittany Miller Lappano, 4 years ago): The customer service at this store is horrible. The organization on the shelves is horrible. There was an article recently about organized crime affecting this store and the shelves are usually empty where you can’t find medicine you need. The pharmacy thinks it’s fine for you to wait 72 hours for a prescription you need urgently. Every time I step into this store, it’s a huge fiasco. It is the worst CVS store I have ever shopped at.

docs.title: Review of CVS Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of CVS Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Allyson Butler, 2 years ago): A shout out to Monique, who treated me at the Minute Clinic today. She was genuinely kind and answered all my questions.She definitely chose the perfect profession for herself!

docs.title: Review of Walgreens Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Walgreens Pharmacy (1 out of 5, by Joseph Weiss, a year ago): Had a bad experience here this week. Got a call from the pharmacist who informed me that I had been overcharged on my credit card, on a prescription. She wanted me to come back to the pharmacy to show PROOF of who I was to have the credit applied. I asked why they needed me as they had my credit card on file and could just simply credit it as is normal with a vendor error. She refused to discuss it telling me that I had to return to get a credit of about $9. I asked again as I am out of town and was summarily refused. Horrible customer service

docs.title: Review of Walgreens Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Walgreens Pharmacy (1 out of 5, by Basir Hickman, 2 years ago): Worst experience ever. Not feeling well, thought I'd come and grab something from the pharmacy to help. Not only was the staff not helpful, but they stood around doing nothing. Took 4 employees to answer one customer, including the young woman ringing up my items. It took her 2 mins to put three items in a bag because she decided a conversation with another employee was more important and couldn't multitask. I thought the 1.3⭐️ rating was a mistake but clearly corporate has given up on this store. Might as well close the doors. 8/11 2:45pm

docs.title: Review of Walgreens Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Walgreens Pharmacy (1 out of 5, by Rallo TV, 4 months ago): If the store is supposed to be open at 7AM I expect the doors to be open at 7AM

docs.title: Review of Walgreens Pharmacy
docs.text:
Google review of Walgreens Pharmacy (1 out of 5, by Ratthee, 3 years ago): Inefficient staff and manager

I asked for a printed receipt, but the staff said that it went to my email. I insisted that i would like to have a printed one because i can't find it in the mailbox. Then she called a manager.

The manager came and said that she changed my profile from digital receipt to a paper one, and then she VOIDED the item. I saw the paper with my own eyes. Then she said she needed to go to print it in the office. 5 mins later, she called that she could not find the receipt (how could you find it if you had voided it?). I asked the staff to return the item and then i  bought it again with a printed receipt. Now i got the receipt. Why can't it be this simple?

It was Friday 22nd Sep 23 at 9:00am

docs.title: Review of Walgreens Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of Walgreens Pharmacy (2 out of 5, by James Parrish, 2 years ago): Not a welcoming place. The store seems a little desolate, and there need to be prices on everything, but there are many missing. I like to shop for value so if you don't know the unit price per ounce for example, you are out of luck! Also the cashiers are demotivated. One woman looked ready for me to leave while I waited for cash back.

docs.title: Review of CVS Pharmacy
docs.text: Google review of CVS Pharmacy (5 out of 5, by Samantha C, a year ago): Probably the nicest CVS location I have visited. The interiors are bright and modern, with no sign of the dreaded aged carpet anywhere. Moreover, an absolute angel of an employee named Acadia (I hope I spelt her name correctly) helped me find a tiny tin of hand balm that I had searched for in three other locations. She went out of her way to offer me help and searched, not giving up until she found the item. Thank you once again!
